## What Daviana is

Daviana is one connected system that runs a whole hair salon. Its five products read and write the same shared client record, so the diary, the colour bowl and the till all agree. It is built and run every day inside six working salons, from London to Saudi Arabia.

- **Daviana Diary** (https://daviana.app/diary/): salon booking software. The appointment diary, till, client records, per-stylist pricing, rota and online booking in one system. Every other Daviana product reads and writes the same client record. £80 a month.
- **Daviana AI Receptionist, Aria** (https://daviana.app/ai-receptionist/): a real AI voice that answers the salon phone when the desk can't. It handles the whole visit and books it straight into the Daviana diary, even while the salon sleeps. £60 a month.
- **Daviana ColorLab** (https://daviana.app/colorlab/): colour management software for hair salons. A Bluetooth precision scale weighs every bowl, a formula can start from a photo, and the true cost of every gram is tied to the booking. £80 a month.
- **Daviana Bar** (https://daviana.app/bar/): drinks ordering for the salon floor. Each drink posts to the client's bill and deducts the stock, to the ingredient, the instant you tap. Included free with the Diary.
- **Daviana Performance** (https://daviana.app/performance/): the team app for salon staff. Live revenue, leaderboards, commission, self-employed settlement and tips for every stylist, read straight from the sales the salon already rang up. Included free with the Diary.

All prices include VAT. No commission on bookings, no per-booking charge, no lock-in. Full details: https://daviana.app/pricing/ . Free trial for a month, no card: https://daviana.app/trial/

## How many salon phone calls go unanswered? What 1,844 real calls show

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/salon-missed-calls-data/
Published: 2026-09-26  ·  Updated: 2026-09-26

On one London salon group's shared phone line, 49% of inbound calls reached nobody in the fortnight before an AI receptionist went live. With the AI answering overflow, that fell to 11%. The desk struggled most at 10am and after 5pm, on Mondays and on Sundays. Most unanswered callers were reconnected within a day, but 15% were not.

### The short answer

- Before an AI receptionist, 49% of calls reached nobody (287 of 585 over 14 days). With one answering overflow, 11% did (140 of 1,259 over 24 days).
- Missed calls are a daytime problem. Only about 10% of calls came before 9am, after 6pm or on a Sunday.
- The desk answered 45% of calls at 10am and 75% at noon. The busiest hour for clients in the chair is the worst hour for the phone.
- Monday was the worst weekday: a person answered 38% of calls, against 71% on Saturday.
- Within 24 hours, 68% of unanswered callers got a call back and 37% rang again and got through. 15% got neither.

Every salon owner suspects the phone rings out more than it should. Very few know the number, because a call nobody answers leaves no trace in the diary. We run our own salons on Daviana, whose phone system logs every call, so we can look.

This is one salon group's data, not an industry survey. We have set out exactly what was counted, and its limits, so you can judge it and compare it with your own.

### What did we count?

Every inbound call to the shared phone line of GA Salons, a group of London salons that runs on Daviana, from 19 August to 25 September 2026 (London time): 1,844 calls from about 900 different numbers. Outbound calls made by the salon are excluded, because a call the salon placed cannot be missed by a client. Each call is counted once, in one of three groups:

- Answered by a person at the front desk.
- Answered by Aria, the salon's AI receptionist, which went live on 2 September and picks up when the desk cannot.
- Reached nobody: the caller hung up or went to voicemail without speaking to anyone.

These are totals only. No client details are used or shown.

### How many salon calls go unanswered?

|  | Calls | Answered by a person | Answered by the AI receptionist | Reached nobody |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before the AI receptionist (19 Aug to 1 Sep, 14 days) | 585 | 298 (51%) | n/a | 287 (49%) |
| With the AI receptionist (2 to 25 Sep, 24 days) | 1,259 | 733 (58%) | 386 (31%) | 140 (11%) |

Before the AI receptionist, roughly one call in two reached nobody. That is not a quiet salon: this is a busy front desk looking after clients in person, where the phone loses every time it clashes with someone standing at the till.

One caution on the first fortnight: it was also the first two weeks on a new phone system, so part of that 49% may be a team getting used to it. The pattern by hour and by day below holds across the whole period.

### When do salon calls go unanswered?

Share of calls answered by a person, by hour of the day (whole period):

| Hour | Calls | Answered by a person |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9am | 220 | 54% |
| 10am | 234 | 45% |
| 11am | 254 | 65% |
| 12pm | 204 | 75% |
| 1pm | 191 | 57% |
| 2pm | 172 | 60% |
| 3pm | 169 | 63% |
| 4pm | 149 | 61% |
| 5pm | 136 | 47% |
| 6pm and later | 67 | 13% |

The two worst hours are the start of the day and the end of it: 10am, when the first clients are being settled and the phone is at its busiest, and 5pm, when the desk is cashing out and rebooking. Lunchtime is the best-covered hour.

And by day of the week:

| Day | Calls | Answered by a person |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | 246 | 38% |
| Tuesday | 366 | 56% |
| Wednesday | 313 | 50% |
| Thursday | 320 | 67% |
| Friday | 312 | 64% |
| Saturday | 203 | 71% |
| Sunday | 84 | 23% |

Monday stands out. It is a day many salons run on a reduced team, but callers do not know that, and it is a heavy day for calls about the week ahead.

### Are missed calls an after-hours problem?

Mostly not. Only about 10% of calls (193 of 1,844) came before 9am, after 6pm or on a Sunday. The other 90% arrived while the salon was open and the desk was busy. When the AI receptionist was live, about a third of its calls (32%) came between 9am and 11am, not in the evening.

So a voicemail message that says "we are closed" is not the fix for most salons. The calls being lost are daytime calls from people who expected someone to pick up.

### What happens to the callers nobody answers?

We followed the 427 calls that reached nobody and checked the next 24 hours for the same number:

- 68% received a call back from the salon.
- 37% rang again and got through.
- 15% did neither: no call back, and no successful call from them.

This salon works its call-back list hard, and that is why most callers were reached. Without a call-back habit, the 15% is the floor, not the ceiling. Those are the callers most likely to have booked somewhere else.

### What should a salon do with this?

- Measure your own line. Most phone systems can export a call log. Count inbound calls by hour and mark which were answered.
- Cover 10am and 5pm. If one person can step away from the chair or the till for those hours, that is where the calls are.
- Look at Mondays. A reduced team on a heavy phone day is the most expensive combination in this data.
- Call back within the hour. Keep a list of missed numbers and work it between clients.
- Put overflow somewhere. A second line, a receptionist service or an AI receptionist that books into your diary. Our guide to AI receptionists for UK salons compares the options.

To put a value on your own missed calls, use the free missed call calculator.

### Questions salon owners ask

#### How many salon calls go unanswered?

In this London salon group's data, 49% of inbound calls reached nobody in the two weeks before an AI receptionist went live, and 11% afterwards. Your own figure depends on your team and your hours; count a week of your call log to find it.

#### What time of day do salons miss the most calls?

Here, 10am (45% answered by a person) and 5pm (47%) were the worst hours, and noon the best (75%). Mondays were the worst weekday (38%).

#### Do most missed salon calls happen after hours?

No. Only about 10% of calls came before 9am, after 6pm or on a Sunday. Most missed calls happened while the salon was open and the desk was busy.

#### Do customers call back if a salon misses their call?

Some do. Within 24 hours, 37% of callers who reached nobody rang again and got through, and 68% were called back by the salon. 15% had neither.

#### Is this data from one salon?

It is one London salon group's shared phone line, 1,844 inbound calls over about five weeks. It is a real, fully counted sample, not an industry-wide survey.

## What is the best booking system for a nail salon in the UK?

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/best-booking-system-nail-salon-uk/
Published: 2026-09-26  ·  Updated: 2026-09-26

The best booking system for a nail salon is the one that books each treatment at its real length, only with technicians who do it, and takes a deposit where a no-show would hurt. If you want new clients from an app, Fresha, Booksy and Treatwell all have marketplaces, for a fee on each new client. If you do not, Timely is the cheapest to start. Daviana suits salons where nails and hair share the same diary.

### The short answer

- Treatment length matters more in nails than almost anywhere: a new full set, an infill and a removal are different lengths and should book that way.
- Only offer a treatment with the technicians who do it. A good system handles that for online booking as well as the desk.
- Take deposits on long treatments. A no-show on a two-hour set costs more than on a quick polish change.
- Marketplace apps bring new clients but charge on each one. Work out what share of your book is regulars before you pay for reach.
- Test the awkward bookings on a demo: a manicure and pedicure together, two clients side by side, and a removal plus a new set.

A nail salon diary looks simple until it is full. Sets, infills, removals, gels and pedicures all run to different lengths, technicians have different skills, and a no-show on a long appointment is an empty chair you cannot fill at short notice. The booking system has to get all of that right without anyone checking it by hand.

We make Daviana, so read our view with that in mind. Every price below for another company comes from its own UK pricing page, checked on 26 September 2026, and is the same set of facts as our UK salon software comparison.

### What does a nail salon need from a booking system?

- Accurate treatment times. Each service should book the time it really takes, so a new set does not get squeezed into an infill slot.
- The right technician. Online booking should only offer each treatment with the people who do it.
- Several services in one visit. A manicure and pedicure, or a removal and a new set, should book as one visit.
- Deposits and no-show rules. Take a deposit on long or expensive treatments, and write down the rule. Our no-show policy template gives wording you can copy.
- A simple till. Services, retail and tips on one bill, with each technician's takings recorded for pay.

### How do the main options compare for a UK nail salon?

|  | Published UK price | New clients and contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresha | £14.95 a month on your own; £9.95 per bookable team member | Marketplace. 20% one-time fee per new marketplace client, minimum £4. No contract |
| Booksy | £40 a month plus £5 per extra team member, plus VAT | Marketplace. New-client fee only with Boost on: 30% of the first visit, minimum £5. No commitment |
| Treatwell | Monthly fee not stated on its pricing page | Marketplace. 35% of a new client's first booking, 0% on repeats, plus VAT. 30 days' notice |
| Timely | From £4, £7 or £9 a week, adjusting with bookings; unlimited team members | No new client fees. No contract, 14 days' notice |
| Daviana | £80 a month including VAT; first month free | No marketplace, no commission. Cancel any month |

Sources for each price are listed in our UK salon software comparison.

### Which one fits your nail salon?

- A solo nail technician building a column. Fresha at £14.95 a month, or Booksy, can bring new clients through their apps. Budget for the new-client fees.
- A small team with a full book of regulars. Timely, from £4 a week with unlimited team members and no new client fees, is the cheapest to start.
- A salon that wants to be listed on Treatwell. Treatwell, if a 35% finder's fee on first bookings works for your prices.
- A salon doing hair and nails together. Daviana keeps both in one diary with each person's skills set, and its AI receptionist can book a manicure while a client's colour develops as one visit. It costs more than Fresha or Timely for a nails-only team.

### How much do new-client fees cost a nail salon? A worked example

Say a marketplace sends you 15 new clients a month, each with a first appointment of £40. At Fresha's 20% that is £120 a month; at Treatwell's 35% plus VAT it is £210 plus VAT. If half of those clients come back regularly, the fee may be good value. If most do not return, you are paying for one-off visits.

These are example figures. Use your own: how many new clients a month, their first-visit value, and how many you keep after three months.

### Questions salon owners ask

#### What is the cheapest booking system for a nail salon in the UK?

On published prices, Timely starts at £4 a week with unlimited team members, and Fresha is £14.95 a month for one person. Check the extras: Timely's price rises with bookings, and Fresha charges 20% on each new marketplace client.

#### Is there a free booking system for nail salons?

Some systems advertise a free start or a free trial, but the costs usually come from card fees, paid texts or a fee on new clients. Compare a year of total cost rather than the headline price.

#### Should a nail salon take deposits?

For long or expensive treatments, usually yes. A deposit makes a no-show less likely and covers part of the empty chair when it happens. Say in writing when it is refundable.

#### Can one booking system handle hair and nails together?

Yes, if it gives each person their own column, knows who does which treatment, and can book two services in one visit. Test a manicure during a colour appointment on the demo.

## What is the best salon software in the UK?

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/best-salon-software-uk/
Published: 2026-09-26  ·  Updated: 2026-09-26

There is no single best salon software. The right one depends on whether you want new clients from a marketplace app, how big your team is, and what you will pay for over a year. Fresha, Treatwell and Booksy bring marketplace clients for a fee. Timely is the cheapest to start without a marketplace. Phorest and SalonIQ are established UK systems for larger salons. Daviana suits salons that also want colour costing and an AI receptionist on the same record.

### The short answer

- Decide first whether you want a marketplace. Fresha, Treatwell and Booksy can bring new clients, and charge a fee on each one; the rest do not.
- Compare a year of total cost, not the headline price: subscription, card fees, paid texts and any new-client commission.
- Read the contract. Most are monthly, but Phorest's UK terms are a one-year contract that renews automatically.
- Hair, nail and beauty salons need the same basics: a diary per staff member, online booking with deposits, and treatment lengths that are right. Test your longest and most awkward service on the demo.
- Ask how your clients and history come across, and how you would take them out again if you left.

Salon software is the diary, the till and the client record your whole day runs on, so switching is a big decision and a bad fit is expensive. Search for the best salon software and most of the lists you find are written by one of the companies on them. This one is too. We make Daviana. So every fact about another company below comes from its own UK pricing or terms page, checked on 26 September 2026 and listed at the end, and we have said plainly where each one is the better choice.

### How do the main UK salon booking systems compare on price?

Prices are as each company publishes them for the UK. Superscripts link to the sources at the end.

|  | Published price | Contract and new-client fees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresha | £14.95 a month on your own; £9.95 a month per bookable team member on Team | No contract. 20% one-time commission on new marketplace clients, minimum £4 |
| Treatwell | Monthly fee not stated on its pricing page | 30 days' notice. 35% on a new marketplace client's first booking, 0% on repeat bookings, 2.5% on online prepayments, all plus VAT |
| Booksy | £40 a month plus £5 a month per extra team member, plus VAT | No commitment. New-client fee only with Boost on: 30% of the first visit, minimum £5 |
| Timely | From £4, £7 or £9 a week by plan, adjusting with bookings; unlimited team members | No contract, 14 days' notice. No new client fees |
| SalonIQ | From £47 a month for a solo stylist; setup from £175 plus VAT | 12-month initial term, then 90 days' written notice, per its terms. No marketplace |
| Phorest | Quote only; no free trial | One year, renewing automatically unless you give two months' notice. No marketplace |
| Daviana | £80 a month including VAT for the diary and till; first month free | No minimum term; cancel any month. No marketplace, no commission on bookings |

### Which salon software suits which salon?

- You want new clients from an app. Fresha, Treatwell and Booksy all run consumer marketplaces. Fresha has the lowest software price and a 20% one-time fee per new marketplace client. Treatwell takes 35% of a new client's first booking, and nothing on repeats. Booksy charges a flat monthly fee and only takes a new-client fee when you switch Boost on. See Fresha alternatives if you are weighing these up.
- You want the lowest price with no marketplace. Timely starts from £4 a week with unlimited team members and no new client fees, though the weekly price rises with bookings. See Daviana vs Timely.
- You are a larger salon or a group that wants an established UK system. Phorest and SalonIQ both fit. Phorest is priced by quote on a one-year contract; SalonIQ publishes a starting price and a setup fee. See Daviana vs Phorest and Daviana vs SalonIQ.
- You want the diary, colour costing and the phone in one system. Daviana's salon booking system is £80 a month including VAT with no marketplace and no minimum term. Its ColorLab weighs and costs colour to the gram, and its AI receptionist books calls into the same diary. It costs more than Fresha or Timely for a small team.

### What should nail and beauty salons look for?

Nail and beauty salons need the same core as hair salons, but the diary gets harder faster. Check these on any demo:

- Treatment lengths that are right. A full set and an infill, or a facial and an add-on, should book the time they really take, including any processing gap.
- Who can do what. Online booking should only offer a treatment with the people who actually do it.
- Two services in one visit. Book a manicure and pedicure together, or two therapists at once, and see whether it creates one visit.
- Deposits and no-show rules. Longer treatments cost more when a client does not turn up. Our salon no-show policy template covers the rules to set.

### What does salon software really cost over a year? A worked example

Take a team of four on Fresha's Team plan: 4 × £9.95 is £39.80 a month for the software. Now say the marketplace sends you 10 new clients a month with a first visit of £60. At 20%, that is £120 a month in commission, so £159.80 a month, or about £1,920 a year, before card fees and paid texts.

These are example figures. Run the same sum with your own numbers for each system on your shortlist: subscription, card processing on your monthly takings, paid texts, any new-client fee, and any setup fee spread over the year. The cheapest headline price is often not the cheapest year.

### What should you ask before you switch?

- How long is the contract, and what does it cost to leave early?
- How are my clients, history, notes and colour formulas moved across, and who does it?
- Can I export everything if I leave, in a format another system can read?
- What are the card processing fees, and do I have to use your payments?
- Who answers the phone when it goes wrong on a Saturday?

We keep a fuller list in 12 questions to ask before switching salon software.

### Questions salon owners ask

#### What is the cheapest salon software in the UK?

On published prices, Timely starts lowest at £4 a week with unlimited team members, and Fresha is £14.95 a month on your own. Both have extra costs to check: Timely's price rises with bookings, and Fresha charges 20% on each new marketplace client.

#### Which salon software has no commission?

Timely says it has no new client fees, and SalonIQ, Phorest and Daviana have no marketplace, so there is no commission. Booksy only charges on new clients when Boost is switched on. Fresha and Treatwell charge on new marketplace clients.

#### Which salon booking systems tie you into a contract?

Phorest's UK terms are a one-year contract that renews automatically unless you give two months' notice. Fresha, Booksy, Timely (14 days' notice), Treatwell (30 days' notice) and Daviana are monthly. SalonIQ's terms set a 12-month initial term, then 90 days' written notice.

#### What is the best booking system for a nail salon in the UK?

The one that books your treatments at the right length with the right technician, and handles two services in one visit. If you want marketplace clients, look at Fresha, Treatwell and Booksy; if you do not, Timely, SalonIQ, Phorest and Daviana. Test your longest and most awkward treatment on a demo before you decide.

#### Can I move my clients from my current salon software?

Usually yes, but what moves depends on what your current system lets you export. Ask any new supplier to look at a real export before you sign. The Daviana team moves your clients and prices across for you.

## What is the best AI receptionist for a UK salon?

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/best-ai-receptionist-for-salons-uk/
Published: 2026-09-26  ·  Updated: 2026-09-26

The best AI receptionist for your salon is the one that books straight into the diary you already use. Treatwell's books into the Treatwell calendar, Salon Agent books into Phorest, Meevo and Square, Zenoti's works inside Zenoti, and Daviana's Aria books into the Daviana diary. After that, compare how it handles multi-service visits, prices, and the calls it should hand to a person.

### The short answer

- An AI receptionist answers the salon phone with a natural voice when nobody on the desk can, and books, moves or cancels appointments during the call.
- The deciding question is the diary. One that books live into your booking system is a receptionist; one that only takes a message is voicemail with better manners.
- For UK salons the realistic shortlist is Treatwell (for Treatwell partners), Salon Agent (Phorest, Meevo, Square), Zenoti, Qlient and Daviana Aria.
- Nail and beauty salons should test multi-service bookings hardest: a gel manicure while colour develops, or two therapists for one client.
- Work out what unanswered calls cost you first. If the number is small, a better voicemail message may be enough.

Salon phones ring when everyone is busy: mid-foil, mid-gel, mid-facial, and after close. Most of those callers do not leave a message. They ring the next salon. An AI receptionist exists to catch those calls and turn them into bookings.

This guide compares the options UK hair, nail and beauty salons are most likely to be shown. The competitor facts come from each company's own website or, for Treatwell, its launch coverage, checked on 26 September 2026 and listed at the end. We make one of the options, Aria, so we have said plainly where each of the others is the better fit.

### What does an AI receptionist for a salon actually do?

It answers the salon number with a natural voice, understands what the caller wants, and deals with it on the call. For a salon that means:

- checking who is free for the service and offering real slots,
- booking, moving or cancelling the appointment,
- answering the everyday questions: prices, opening hours, parking, how long a service takes,
- handing over to a person, or taking a message, when the caller needs one.

The difference between tools is mostly in the first two. An AI that can only take a message saves you listening to voicemail. An AI that books into your live diary saves the booking.

### How do the main salon AI receptionists compare?

Prices are as each company publishes them. Superscripts link to the sources at the end.

|  | Published price | Books into | Built for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Treatwell AI Receptionist | From £69 a month, three tiers | The Treatwell calendar | Treatwell partner salons across its European markets |
| Salon Agent AI | $200 a month for the 24/7 call agent, $250 with webchat (USD) | Phorest, Meevo and Square live; with Fresha, Booksy, Vagaro and others it captures the booking for your team | Salons and spas |
| Zenoti AI Receptionist | Not published | Zenoti; calls are forwarded to a Zenoti number | Salons, spas, medspas and other Zenoti businesses |
| Qlient | Not published | Schedules, reschedules and cancels; systems not listed on its homepage | Beauty salons and spas |
| Daviana Aria | £60 a month including VAT, first month free | The Daviana diary, live, the same one the front desk uses | Salons that run on Daviana |

General-purpose AI receptionists also exist, such as Aira from $24.95 a month (USD), which connects to Google Calendar, Outlook and Cal.com. They suit a business with one calendar. A salon diary with a column per stylist and services of different lengths usually needs a salon-specific tool.

### Which one fits your salon?

- You are a Treatwell partner and run your diary in Treatwell. Treatwell's own receptionist manages appointments in that calendar and starts at £69 a month. That is the obvious first look.
- You are on Phorest, Meevo or Square. Salon Agent books against your live availability in those three and publishes its prices. Remember they are in US dollars.
- You are on Fresha, Booksy or another system without a live integration. Check exactly what happens on the call. Salon Agent, for example, captures the booking and hands it to your team for those systems, so a person still has to put it in the diary.
- You run on Zenoti. Zenoti's own receptionist is built into the platform; ask for the price, as it is not published.
- You want the phone, the diary and the till in one system. Aria books straight into the Daviana diary, re-checks the slot at the moment of booking, and saves a note of the call on the client's record. If you are staying on another booking system, Aria is not the right choice.

### What should nail and beauty salons check?

Nail and beauty diaries are harder for an AI than a single haircut, because one visit often means two services, two people, or a service that has to fit around another. Test these on any demo:

- Two services in one visit. Ask for a gel manicure and a pedicure together, or nails while hair colour develops, and see whether it offers one visit or two unrelated bookings.
- The right therapist for the treatment. Not every therapist does every treatment. The AI should only offer people who actually do the service.
- Treatment length. A full set of extensions and an infill are different lengths. Check it books the time the treatment really takes.
- Questions it should not answer alone. Anything about allergies, skin reactions or aftercare should go to a person, and so should anything about money.

Aria composes a visit rather than a single slot, for example nails while the colour develops or two specialists staggered, and checks each service for who is actually free before booking it as one visit.

### How much are unanswered calls costing you? A worked example

Take three numbers from your own phone bill and diary: how many calls ring out in a week, what share of callers wanted to book, and your average booking value. Say 30 calls a week ring out, half were booking calls, and a booking is worth £60. If a third of those callers would have booked with you, that is 5 bookings and £300 a week, or roughly £1,300 a month.

These are example figures, not industry averages. Put your own into the free missed call calculator, which shows every assumption and does not ask for an email. If the answer is less than an AI receptionist costs, answer more calls yourself first. There is more on what happens to after-hours salon calls in our journal.

### Questions salon owners ask

#### How much does an AI receptionist cost for a salon in the UK?

On published prices, Treatwell's starts at £69 a month for its partner salons, Salon Agent's call agent is $200 a month in US dollars, and Daviana's Aria is £60 a month including VAT. Zenoti and Qlient do not publish prices. General AI receptionists start lower but do not connect to a salon diary.

#### Will an AI receptionist book into my existing booking system?

Only if it integrates with it. Salon Agent books live into Phorest, Meevo and Square, Treatwell's books into the Treatwell calendar, Zenoti's works inside Zenoti, and Aria books into the Daviana diary. For other systems, check whether the booking is made on the call or passed to your team to enter later.

#### Is there an AI receptionist for nail salons?

Yes. The salon-specific tools cover nail salons too. The thing to test is multi-service booking: ask for a manicure and pedicure together and see whether it books one visit with the right technicians.

#### Will clients know they are talking to an AI?

Most tools use a natural voice, and many callers will not notice. We think it is better not to set out to trick anyone; in practice most callers want an appointment, a price or your opening hours, and care more about getting them quickly than about who answered.

#### Can I hear an AI receptionist before I buy?

Ask any supplier for a live test on your own salon. For Aria you can do it now: use the call-me form on the AI receptionist page and Aria reads your salon's website, then rings your mobile and answers as your salon, or ring the demo line on +44 7460 096908.

- Aira: AI agents for service businesses (pricing, calendar integrations) — checked 2026-09-26

## What is the best hair colour management software for UK salons?

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/best-hair-colour-management-software/
Published: 2026-09-26  ·  Updated: 2026-09-26

There are four serious options in the UK: Vish, SalonScale, Color Bar Manager and Daviana ColorLab. They all weigh or track the colour you mix and show what it cost. The best one for you depends mostly on your booking system. Vish plugs into systems such as Phorest and SalonIQ, SalonScale connects directly to Square, Color Bar Manager can start without a scale, and ColorLab shares one record with the Daviana diary and till.

### The short answer

- Hair colour management software weighs each bowl, saves the formula to the client and shows what the colour cost, so you can stop overmixing and charge for what was used.
- The first question is not features but fit: which booking system you are keeping, and whether the colour charge will reach the client's bill without retyping.
- Three of the four publish prices in US dollars only. Convert them, add VAT, and add scales and tablets before you compare with a UK price.
- Plan for adoption. Software that needs every bowl weighed only pays if the team weighs every bowl.
- Work out what a head of colour costs you today before you buy anything. That is the number the software is meant to reduce.

Most salons know their colour bill and almost none know what a single head of colour costs them. Colour gets mixed by eye, the leftover goes down the sink, and the product used on a long root and lengths never quite makes it onto the bill. Hair colour management software exists to close that gap.

This guide compares the four tools UK salon owners are most likely to be looking at. The competitor facts come from each company's own pricing and product pages, checked on 26 September 2026 and listed at the end. We make one of the four, ColorLab, so we have said plainly where each of the others is the better choice.

### What does hair colour management software actually do?

At the colour bar, the stylist opens the client, picks the shades and pours onto a connected scale. The software records the grams of each product and developer, saves that formula to the client, and works out what the bowl cost from your product prices. Most tools then add three things on top:

- Formula history, so the next visit starts from exactly what was used last time, whoever is on the chair.
- Charging, so colour used beyond what the service includes can be added to the bill.
- Stock, so reordering follows what was really poured rather than a guess.

The saving comes from two places: less colour mixed and thrown away, and fewer services where the colour used was never charged. There is more on where that money goes in how much hair colour is your salon really wasting?

### How do Vish, SalonScale, Color Bar Manager and ColorLab compare?

Prices are as each company publishes them. Superscripts link to the sources at the end.

|  | Published price | Scales | Works with | Devices |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vish | $40 to $365 a month by plan (USD), Enterprise on quote, plus a one-time setup and education fee | Extra, $195 each, and a tablet per scale | Your existing salon software, including Phorest, SalonIQ, Shortcuts, Zenoti, Square and Boulevard | iPad or Android tablet |
| SalonScale | $49 to $199 a month by number of stylists (USD) | Use a scale you already have; a free precision scale with annual billing | Connects directly to Square; designed to sit alongside other systems | Mobile app |
| Color Bar Manager | $15 a week, $47 a month or $464 a year (USD); custom for groups | Not required to start; add them later | Works alongside your existing salon software | Web and iOS |
| Daviana ColorLab | £80 a month including VAT, first month free | A Bluetooth precision scale guides every pour to the gram | Part of Daviana: the same record as the Daviana diary and till | iOS and web |

### Which one fits your salon?

Start from the booking system you are keeping, then from how your team works.

- You are staying on Phorest, SalonIQ, Shortcuts or Zenoti. Vish lists integrations with all of them, and a paid Sync+ add-on for Phorest salons. It is the most established choice for a salon that is not changing its diary. See our ColorLab vs Vish comparison.
- You take payments on Square. SalonScale integrates with Square directly, publishes simple per-stylist-band pricing, and lets you use a scale you already own.
- You want to start without changing habits on day one. Color Bar Manager is built to be useful before every stylist weighs every bowl, starts at $15 a week, and has a 30-day money-back guarantee.
- You want colour on the same record as your diary and till. Daviana ColorLab reads the day's colour clients and per-stylist prices from the Daviana diary and, where a salon turns it on, posts the colour charge back to the appointment. There is no sync to keep in step, the price is in pounds with VAT included, and a formula can start from a photo of the hair.

If none of those describes you, the tie-breaker is usually the one your team will actually use at 4pm on a Saturday.

### What should you check before you buy?

- The real monthly price in pounds. Three of the four publish US dollar prices. Convert, add VAT where it applies, and add scales, tablets and any setup fee.
- Whether the charge reaches the bill. Weighing without charging only saves the overmix. Ask exactly how the extra colour gets onto the client's bill in your booking system, and whether anyone has to retype it.
- Your colour brands. Check the shade library covers the lines you use, including any own-label colour.
- What happens to formulas if you leave. Your clients' colour history is the most valuable data in the salon. Ask how you would export it.
- How the team will use it. A scale by every mixing station and a two-minute routine matter more than any feature on the list.

### How much could it save your salon? A worked example

Take two figures from your own records: what you spend on professional colour in a month, and how many colour services you do. Say it is £2,000 across 250 services, which is £8 a service on average. If weighing shows that one bowl in ten is overmixed by a quarter, that is roughly £50 a month of colour in the sink. If one service in twenty uses more colour than the price includes and it never reaches the bill, add those services at your extra-colour charge.

These are example figures, not industry averages. Replace them with yours in our free salon colour cost calculator, which works from your own spend and does not ask for an email. If the answer is less than the software costs, you do not need it yet.

### Questions salon owners ask

#### Do I need a special scale for colour management software?

It depends on the tool. Vish sells its own scales at $195 each and needs a tablet per scale. SalonScale lets you use a scale you already have and includes a free precision scale with annual billing. Color Bar Manager does not need a scale to start. Daviana ColorLab uses a Bluetooth precision scale that guides each pour to the gram.

#### Which hair colour management software is cheapest?

On published prices, Color Bar Manager starts lowest at $15 a week or $47 a month, and Vish Solo is $40 a month for a single stylist before scales and setup. For a team, compare the plan for your number of stylists plus hardware, converted to pounds with VAT, against Daviana ColorLab at £80 a month including VAT.

#### Does colour management software work with Phorest?

Vish lists Phorest among its integrations and offers a paid Sync+ add-on for Phorest salons. SalonScale integrates directly with Square only. Color Bar Manager says it works alongside existing salon software. Daviana ColorLab is part of Daviana rather than an add-on to Phorest.

#### Can I charge clients for the extra colour they use?

That is one of the main reasons to weigh. Vish sends exact usage and prices to the front desk, SalonScale connects to Square at checkout, and Daviana ColorLab can post the colour charge back to the appointment. Whichever you use, put your extra-colour policy on your price list so clients are not surprised.

#### Is colour management software worth it for a solo stylist?

Sometimes. A solo stylist knows their own habits, so the saving is smaller than in a team. Run your own figures through a colour cost calculator first; if the monthly saving is less than the subscription, a notebook and a kitchen scale will do for now.

## How should a UK salon structure stylist commission?

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/salon-commission-structure/
Published: 2026-09-24  ·  Updated: 2026-09-24

Most UK salons pay employed stylists in one of three ways: a flat percentage of service takings, a basic wage plus commission on takings above a target, or tiered rates that rise as takings rise. Pay retail at its own rate, agree up front whether product cost comes off, and check every pay period still clears minimum wage.

### The short answer

- There are three common structures: a flat percentage of service takings, a basic wage plus commission above a target, and tiered rates. Each moves the risk of a quiet month to a different person.
- Run your own last two months through each structure before you choose. The wage cost as a share of takings is the number that decides whether it works.
- Pay retail at a separate rate. Mixing it into service takings hides whether anyone is actually selling.
- Commission counts towards minimum wage but tips do not, and the check is made each pay period, not averaged over the year.
- Write the structure down, including whether product cost comes off, before a stylist starts. Most commission disputes come from a rule nobody wrote down.

Commission is the part of salon pay that causes the most arguments, and most of those arguments start with a structure that was agreed verbally years ago and never written down. Picking a structure deliberately, and testing it on your own numbers first, saves a lot of awkward conversations later.

This guide is for employed stylists. Self-employed and chair-rental stylists are a different arrangement, covered briefly near the end.

## What are the main salon commission structures?

Nearly every UK salon uses one of these three, sometimes with retail commission added on top.

| Structure | How it works | Who carries a quiet month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat percentage | The stylist earns a fixed share of every pound of service takings, with no basic wage. | The stylist, until pay falls below minimum wage, then the salon has to top up. |
| Basic plus commission above a target | A fixed basic wage, plus a percentage of service takings above a monthly target. | The salon. The basic is paid whatever the diary looks like. |
| Tiered | The rate rises in steps as takings pass set thresholds, for example one rate on the first slice and a higher rate above it. | Shared. Busy stylists earn more per pound, quiet months pay the lower rate. |

None of them is right for every salon. A new stylist building a column usually needs the security of a basic. A senior stylist with a full diary often prefers a structure where a busy month is visibly rewarded.

## How do you work out which structure you can afford? A worked example

Take one stylist and write down four figures from your own records:

- service takings in a busy month,
- service takings in a quiet month,
- retail sales in a typical month,
- the hours they are contracted to work in a month.

Say the busy month is £7,500, the quiet month is £5,000, retail is £500 and hours are 160. Here are three structures, run on both months, before retail:

| Structure | Busy month (£7,500) | Quiet month (£5,000) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: 30% of service takings, no basic | £2,250 (30% of takings) | £1,500 (30%), about £9.38 an hour |
| B: £2,200 basic plus 15% above £6,000 | £2,200 + £225 = £2,425 (32%) | £2,200 (44%) |
| C: 25% on the first £5,000, 35% above it | £1,250 + £875 = £2,125 (28%) | £1,250 (25%), about £7.81 an hour |

The busy month looks similar across all three. The quiet month is where they split. Structures A and C pay well under the National Living Wage for 160 hours, so the salon has to top the stylist up anyway, and the percentage in brackets understates what the month really cost. Structure B is safe for the stylist but costs the salon 44% of takings in a slow month.

Add retail at, say, 10%, and the stylist earns another £50 in every structure. Keeping it separate means you can see who is selling, which a single blended rate hides.

Now replace the example figures with yours. The question to answer is simple: across a busy and a quiet month, what share of service takings goes on this stylist's pay, and can the salon live with the worse of the two?

## What goes wrong with tiered commission?

Tiers are popular because they reward a full column, but one detail decides whether they work: does the higher rate apply only to takings above the threshold, or to everything once the threshold is passed?

In the example above, 35% applies only to the slice above £5,000. If instead the whole month jumped to 35% once the stylist passed £5,000, a stylist on £4,990 would earn £1,247.50 and one on £5,010 would earn £1,753.50. That is £506 more pay for £20 more takings. Cliff edges like that encourage moving appointments between months and leave the stylist who falls just short feeling cheated. If you use tiers, apply each rate to its own slice and write that down.

## Should commission come off takings before or after product cost?

Some salons pay commission on gross service takings. Others take the cost of the colour used off first, on the basis that a stylist who overmixes should not be paid on product that went down the sink.

Either can be fair, but the second only works if the cost is measured. In the busy month above, if £600 of colour is deducted first under structure A, commission falls from £2,250 to £2,070. A stylist will accept that £180 if they can see what was used on each client. They will not accept a flat amount knocked off every colour service. Weighing the bowl to the gram, which is what [ColorLab](https://daviana.app/colorlab/) does, turns the deduction into a record rather than a guess, and our [colour cost calculator](https://daviana.app/tools/colour-cost-calculator/) shows what a typical head of colour costs you before you decide.

## Does commission have to meet minimum wage?

Yes, for employed stylists. [GOV.UK guidance on calculating the minimum wage](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/calculating-the-minimum-wage/calculating-the-minimum-wage) says sales commission and other performance-related pay count towards minimum wage pay, but tips, gratuities and service charges do not. The check is made over each pay reference period, which is never longer than a month. A great December does not make up for a thin January.

Holiday pay is the other rule salons often miss. [GOV.UK guidance on holiday pay](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights/holiday-pay-the-basics) says at least 4 weeks of statutory holiday for regular-hours workers must be paid at the normal rate of pay, and the normal rate includes commission. A stylist paid mostly in commission should not see their pay collapse when they take a week off.

This is a practical summary, not legal or tax advice. Check the current minimum wage rates for each stylist's age on GOV.UK, and ask an accountant or employment adviser if you are unsure.

## What about self-employed and chair-rental stylists?

Self-employed stylists are usually not paid commission by the salon at all. They keep their own takings and pay the salon rent, or a share, for the chair. Whether someone is genuinely self-employed depends on how they actually work, not on what the contract calls them, and HMRC has a [tool to check employment status](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-employment-status-for-tax). Many salons run both arrangements side by side, which is exactly where a spreadsheet starts to struggle.

## What should your salon software do for you?

Whatever structure you pick, it has to be calculated the same way every month without someone rebuilding it by hand. Things worth checking in any system:

- Can you set a service rate, a separate retail rate, and override the rate for particular service categories?
- Does it support tiers, and are they applied slice by slice?
- Is commission worked out from the same diary and till the desk uses, not an export?
- Can employed commission and self-employed settlement be handled side by side?

In [Daviana Performance](https://daviana.app/performance/), commission levels combine a flat service rate, tiered retail commission and category overrides, and a running commission ledger builds itself from every sale, with employed rates and self-employed settlement side by side. Stylists see their own numbers as the month goes, which is why we think [live commission tracking](https://daviana.app/blog/live-commission-tracking/) matters as much as the structure itself.

## Questions salon owners ask

### What is a normal commission rate for a hairdresser in the UK?

There is no single standard rate. It depends on whether you also pay a basic wage, whether product cost comes off first, and what share of service takings your salon can afford to spend on wages. Work backwards from that share using your own takings, rather than copying another salon's percentage.

### Does commission count towards the National Minimum Wage?

Yes. GOV.UK guidance says sales commission and other performance-related pay count towards minimum wage pay. Tips, gratuities and service charges do not. The check is made over each pay reference period, which is never longer than a month, so a strong month cannot cover for a quiet one.

### Should holiday pay include commission?

For employed stylists, yes. GOV.UK guidance says at least 4 weeks of statutory holiday for regular-hours workers must be paid at the normal rate of pay, and the normal rate includes commission. For irregular-hours workers, all statutory leave is paid at the normal rate.

### Can a salon deduct product costs before paying commission?

Yes, if it is written into the stylist's pay terms before they start and the pay still clears minimum wage. It is only fair when the cost is measured, for example by weighing colour to the gram, rather than a flat guess taken off every colour service.

## What should a salon no-show policy say? A UK template you can copy

Source: https://daviana.app/blog/salon-no-show-policy/
Published: 2026-09-22  ·  Updated: 2026-09-22

A good salon no-show policy says four things in plain words: how much notice a client must give to cancel, what happens if they give less, what happens if they do not turn up, and which bookings need a deposit. Keep it short, show it before the client books, and never charge more than the empty chair actually costs you.

### The short answer

- A no-show policy only works if the client saw it before they booked. A rule they first hear about when you charge them is an argument, not a policy.
- Four parts are enough: the notice window, the late cancellation charge, the no-show charge, and which services need a deposit.
- Take deposits on the long, expensive bookings that are hard to refill at short notice, not on every trim.
- In the UK a cancellation charge has to be fair and transparent. A fee well above what you actually lose is at risk of being unenforceable.
- Enforce it the same way for everyone, but give the desk one discretionary waiver per client for genuine emergencies.

Every salon owner knows the feeling: a three-hour colour slot at 10am, a stylist ready, a bowl about to be mixed, and nobody walks in. The chair time is gone, and unlike a product on a shelf, it cannot be sold tomorrow.

A written no-show policy will not stop every missed appointment. What it does is turn an awkward conversation into a rule the client already agreed to, and give your desk something to point at.

## What should a salon no-show policy include?

Keep it to four parts. Anything longer does not get read, and a policy the client did not read is hard to enforce.

1. **The notice window.** How many hours before the appointment a client can cancel or move it without charge. 24 or 48 hours is typical.
2. **The late cancellation charge.** What happens if they cancel inside the window. Usually the deposit is kept, or a percentage of the booking is charged.
3. **The no-show charge.** What happens if they simply do not arrive. Usually the same as a late cancellation, sometimes higher.
4. **Which bookings need a deposit.** A clear rule, such as all colour services or any booking over a set value.

Add one line on lateness (for example, arriving more than 15 minutes late may mean a shorter service or rebooking) and one line on how to cancel. That is the whole policy.

## Is there a salon no-show policy template I can copy?

Yes. Edit the numbers in square brackets to suit your salon, then put it on your booking page, in your confirmation email and on the wall at reception.

> **Cancellations and missed appointments**
>
> We keep your time just for you, so we ask for at least [48] hours’ notice if you need to cancel or move your appointment. You can do this [online, by phone or by replying to your confirmation].
>
> A deposit of [25]% is taken when you book any [colour service / appointment of £100 or more]. It comes off your bill on the day.
>
> If you cancel with less than [48] hours’ notice, your deposit is kept. If there is no deposit on your booking, a charge of [50]% of the service price may apply.
>
> If you miss your appointment without letting us know, your deposit is kept and we may ask for a deposit on future bookings.
>
> If you are running more than [15] minutes late, please call us. We will do our best, but we may need to shorten your service or rebook you.
>
> We understand emergencies happen. Please talk to us.

The last line matters more than it looks. It tells the client the policy is about protecting chair time, not about catching them out, and it gives the desk room to use judgement.

## How much deposit should a salon take? A worked example

Start from your own numbers, not from what another salon charges. Take last month and write down three figures:

- the number of no-shows,
- the average value of a booking that did not turn up,
- the number of late cancellations the desk could not refill, and their average value.

Say you had 12 no-shows averaging £85, and 6 unfilled late cancellations averaging £70. That is 12 × £85 = £1,020 plus 6 × £70 = £420, so £1,440 of chair time lost in a month, or £17,280 over a year if the month is typical.

Now look at where that money sits. In most salons it is concentrated in the long bookings: full head colour, balayage, extensions, restyles. A cut and finish that goes missing is irritating but can often be refilled from a walk-in or a waiting list. A three-hour colour slot at short notice usually cannot.

| Rule you might set | What it covers | What you keep from one no-show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No deposit under £100 | Cuts, blow-dries, toners | Nothing, rely on the notice window |
| 25% on bookings of £100 or more | Most colour work | £35 on a £140 booking |
| 50% on bookings of £200 or more | Long colour, extensions | £110 on a £220 booking |

In the example, if 5 of the 12 no-shows were £140 colour bookings, a 25% deposit keeps 5 × £35 = £175 that month. That will not cover the whole loss, and it is not supposed to. The bigger effect is that a client who has paid something upfront has a reason to pick up the phone when plans change, and a phone call 48 hours out gives the desk time to refill the chair.

## Is it legal to charge a no-show fee in the UK?

Generally yes, with two conditions. First, the client must have been told before they booked. A term they only discover afterwards is unlikely to hold. Second, the charge must be fair. The Consumer Rights Act 2015 says terms in consumer contracts must be fair and transparent, and the Competition and Markets Authority’s [guidance on unfair contract terms (CMA37)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/unfair-contract-terms-cma37) treats cancellation charges that go well beyond the business’s likely loss as a warning sign.

In practice that means:

- keep the charge in proportion to the chair time you lose, which is why a percentage of the booking is easier to defend than a large flat fee;
- show the policy on the booking page and in the confirmation, not only on a sign in the salon;
- refund a deposit if you are the one who cancels or cannot deliver the service;
- keep a record of when the client booked, what they were shown and when they cancelled.

This is a practical summary, not legal advice. If you are unsure about a specific charge, check the guidance or ask a solicitor.

## How do you enforce a no-show policy without losing good clients?

The policy is the easy part. Applying it consistently at the desk is where most salons give up, usually because the person on reception does not want an awkward conversation with a regular.

A few habits make it easier:

- **Take the deposit at booking, not afterwards.** Asking for money after a missed appointment is a confrontation. A deposit already paid is simply kept.
- **Remind clients before the window closes.** A reminder the day before a 48-hour window has already shut is too late to be useful. Send it before the notice period starts.
- **Give the desk one waiver per client, and log it.** Genuine emergencies get goodwill. The second missed appointment does not, and the record shows it was the second.
- **Make cancelling easy.** If the only way to cancel is a phone that nobody answers after 6pm, clients who meant to give notice end up as no-shows.

That last point is the one salons most often miss. A client who tries to cancel at 9pm and reaches voicemail has done the right thing, and still leaves you with an empty chair unless someone hears the message in time. Our [piece on after-hours salon calls](https://daviana.app/blog/after-hours-salon-calls/) covers how much of that happens outside opening hours.

## What should your booking system do for you?

A policy lives or dies on whether the [booking system](https://daviana.app/diary/) backs it up without the desk having to remember. The things worth checking in any salon software:

- Can it take a deposit when the client books online, with rules by percentage and booking value?
- When a client cancels, can the desk choose to keep or refund the deposit, with the reason recorded?
- Does an unpaid deposit hold release the slot automatically, so the diary is not blocked by a booking nobody paid for?
- Is a no-show a status on the appointment, so you can see who has missed before and report on it?

In Daviana, deposits are taken at online booking into the same diary the desk uses, and are set by percentage, minimum and booking threshold. On cancellation the desk chooses whether to retain or refund the deposit, unpaid deposit holds expire on their own, and no-shows and cancellations show up in reporting. If a client calls to cancel at the last minute, [Aria, the AI receptionist](https://daviana.app/ai-receptionist/), reads back the real appointment and offers to reschedule; on anything to do with fees it takes a message for the team rather than deciding. If you are comparing systems, our [questions to ask before switching salon software](https://daviana.app/blog/questions-before-switching-salon-software/) are a good place to start.

## Questions salon owners ask

### Can a UK salon charge a client for not turning up?

Yes, if the charge was clearly shown to the client before they booked and it is fair. Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 a cancellation or no-show charge should broadly reflect what the salon loses, such as the value of chair time it could not resell. A charge far above that loss risks being treated as an unfair term.

### How much deposit should a salon take?

Most salons take a percentage of the booking, often somewhere between 20 and 50 per cent, and only on services that are long, expensive or hard to refill at short notice. A flat rule such as 25 per cent on bookings of £100 or more is easy for clients to understand and for the desk to apply.

### How much notice should a salon ask for when a client cancels?

24 or 48 hours is the most common window. Pick the shortest window in which your desk can realistically refill the slot. Long colour appointments usually justify 48 hours; a cut and finish can often be refilled with 24.

### Should a salon charge a regular client who misses one appointment?

The policy should apply to everyone, but it helps to give the desk one discretionary waiver per client for a genuine emergency, logged against the client record. That keeps goodwill with loyal clients while making repeat no-shows visible.
